videos.title: ONLY WOMEN ARE ALLOWED HERE?! FACT CHECK
videos.description:
Is there really a women-only city in Oregon where no man is allowed? We fact-check the viral "Woman's Land" claims: zero crime, 1,000 acres, no boys, unanimous vote.

The viral version says one city, 1,000 acres, 40+ women and zero crime for 48 years. The real story: in the 1970s, women in southern Oregon bought eight small rural farms, roughly 7 to 150 acres each, home to about 4 to 30 women. Rules on boys differed farm to farm. At OWL Farm, any woman could move in for about 22 years. Its 147 acres, bought in 1976, are still held in trust for women today.

videos.title: There is another earth?!
videos.description:
Earth's closest twin, Proxima b, is just 4.2 light-years away. So why can't we go? The nearest Earth-like planet explained in 60 seconds.

Proxima b is a rocky planet at least about as heavy as Earth, orbiting in the habitable zone of Proxima Centauri, the closest star to the Sun. Even light takes 4.2 years to get there; Voyager 1, at about 60,000 km/h, would need roughly 76,000 years. A year on Proxima b lasts just 11.2 days, and it orbits about 20 times closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun, so one side probably always faces it. Its red dwarf star also throws violent flares: in May 2019 it got about 14,000 times brighter in ultraviolet in seconds. Whether the planet still has an atmosphere is not yet known.

videos.title: WHY DO STARS TWINKLE?!
videos.description:
Why do stars twinkle, and why don't planets? The twinkle isn't the star at all: it's about 100 km of moving air above your head.

Starlight from Sirius travels about 8.6 years to reach you, then gets bent around by warm and cold pockets of air in roughly its last third of a millisecond. Stars are so far away that their light arrives as a single point, so every pocket of air shoves it brighter, dimmer, left and right. Planets are much closer and show a tiny disc, so they usually shine steady. That's why astronomers climb: Chile's Atacama Desert hosts telescopes over 2,600 m up, India's Hanle observatory in Ladakh sits at about 4,500 m inside India's first dark sky reserve, Europe's new 39 m telescope will reshape a mirror about 1,000 times a second, and Hubble simply orbits about 480 km up, above the air.

Sources:
https://www.britannica.com/science/Why-Do-Stars-Twinkle

videos.title: WHAT IF THERE IS SNOWFALL IN DELHI? 🤯
videos.description:
What if the Himalayas were in central India? How one 2,400 km mountain wall decides India's monsoon, why Ladakh is a cold desert, and why Delhi could end up just as dry.

Every summer the monsoon slams into the Himalayas, rises and rains on the south side, so Leh, behind the wall, gets only about 100 mm a year while Delhi gets around 800. Drag the range south onto the Tropic of Cancer and the south gets soaked, while Delhi sits in the rain shadow, open to icy winds from Central Asia. (A thought experiment: the "could" is ours.) The twist: the wall isn't moving south. India is pushing north into it, about 5 cm a year.

videos.description:
Chimborazo vs Everest: which mountain is really closest to space and the Sun? Everest is the highest above sea level, but Ecuador's Chimborazo is the farthest point from Earth's centre.

Earth spins, so it bulges at the equator: the equator sits about 21 km farther from the centre than the poles. Chimborazo stands just 1 degree from the equator, so its peak is about 6,384 km from Earth's centre, more than 2 km farther out than Everest's (about 6,382 km), even though it is about 2,600 m shorter. Measured from the centre, Everest isn't even in the top 20, and Kilimanjaro beats it too.

This is the only country on Earth where every bit of land sits above 1,000 metres, and it's completely surrounded by South Africa.

In 1824, chief Moshoeshoe led his people up Thaba Bosiu, a flat-topped mountain ringed by cliffs that was never taken by force. videos.title: Mariana Trench Is 10,927 m Deep… Maybe 😳
videos.description:
How deep is the Mariana Trench? The Challenger Deep was re-mapped in 2026 at about 10,927 metres, but 150 years of measurements still don't agree.

In 1875, sailors on HMS Challenger lowered a weighted rope and hit bottom at about 8,184 m. Sonar later gave 10,863 m (1951) and 11,033 m (1957). Sonar times an echo, and the speed of sound in seawater shifts with temperature, salt and pressure, so a small error moves the bottom. A Japanese team on R/V Hakuho-maru re-mapped it with five sound-speed models: best estimate 10,927 m, with the models alone spanning about 18 m. In 1984 another Japanese survey got 10,920 m. The deepest point on Earth is less a number than a range.

videos.title: WHY IS AMERICA COLDER THAN LONDON 🇬🇧🤯🇺🇸
videos.description:
Why is America colder than Europe? London is further north than all 48 mainland US states, yet New York is about 5°C colder in January. Is it really the Gulf Stream?
The Gulf Stream helps, but the bigger reasons are the wind and the Rocky Mountains.

London sits at 51.5°N, north of every point in the mainland USA. In January it averages about +5°C; New York (40.7°N) is about 1°C, and Calgary, on London's latitude, about −8°C. In 2002, scientists at Columbia University ran climate-model experiments: the ocean's heat transport warms Europe by only a few degrees, and warms both sides of the Atlantic roughly alike. Most of the gap comes from the westerly winds (Europe's air has crossed an ocean that stores summer heat; New York's has crossed a frozen continent) and from the Rockies bending the jet stream. Scientists still debate the exact split.

videos.title: Halley's Comet Is 5 Billion km Away. So Why Is It Here?
videos.description:
Halley's Comet is hitting your sky right now: the Orionid meteor shower is Halley's dust. Here's how a comet over 5 billion km away still reaches Earth.

Every 76 years or so, Halley swings past the Sun and sheds dust that stays spread along its orbit. Earth crosses that trail twice a year: in May (the Eta Aquariids) and in October (the Orionids). Halley orbits the "wrong way", so we hit its dust head-on at about 66 km per second, roughly Delhi to Mumbai in 17 seconds. Each sand-sized grain burns up around 100 km above you, best seen after midnight from both hemispheres. Halley itself is due back in July 2061.

videos.title: Earth Had 6 Kinds of Humans at Once 🤯 #geography #dna #neanderthal
videos.description:
How many human species lived on Earth at the same time? About 100,000 years ago there were six, and Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA is still in many people today.

Homo sapiens in Africa, Neanderthals in Europe, Denisovans in Siberia and East Asia, the last Homo erectus on Java, the one-metre "Hobbits" of Flores (Homo floresiensis) and Homo luzonensis in the Philippines, only named in 2019. By about 40,000 years ago the Neanderthals were gone, and one by one the others vanished. But our ancestors had children with them: people with roots in Europe or Asia carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA, and in Papua New Guinea it's up to about 5% Denisovan.

videos.title: Why Bengaluru Has 1,000s of Lakes but No River 🇮🇳
videos.description:
Why does Bengaluru have so many lakes when it has no big river? The history of Bengaluru's lakes, from 9th-century tanks to the Majestic bus stand.

Bengaluru sits on a ridge about 920 m up, with no major river nearby. So for more than 1,100 years, people built earth embankments across the valleys to trap monsoon rain, creating chains of tanks that overflow from one into the next: six cascading chains across three valleys. Kempegowda, who founded the city in 1537, kept building more. Then the city grew over them: from 1973 to 2013, about 79% of its water bodies vanished, and today water is pumped about 100 km from the Kaveri and lifted about 300 m. Some lost lakes are hiding in plain sight: Kanteerava Stadium (Sampangi Lake), KR Market (Siddikatte) and Majestic bus stand (Dharmambudhi).

videos.title: Why Time Zones Looks So Strange 🌍
videos.description:
Earth spins at a steady speed, so why do time zones look like they were drawn by a nervous squirrel? 🌍

Until 1883, every town set its clock by the Sun. Then American railroads reset their clocks on the "Day of Two Noons", and in 1884, 25 nations picked Greenwich as zero. But today's lines are drawn by governments: China runs one time zone across the whole country, France has 12, Samoa deleted a Friday in 2011, and Nepal sits 15 minutes ahead of India.

videos.title: The American Town on Fire for 64 Years 🔥😱
videos.description:
Centralia, Pennsylvania: a coal-mine fire has burned under this US town since 1962, and only 5 people still live there.
Why nobody put it out, why the town was moved instead, and how long the fire could keep burning.

The story goes, in 1962 the town burned its trash in an old mining pit and the fire reached the coal mines below. Flushing it ran out of money after about $42,000. A 1983 federal study put the cost of putting it out at $663 million; Congress gave $42 million to move people instead. About 500 homes and shops were torn down, and in 2002 even the ZIP code went. At its current rate, the fire could burn for another 250 years.

videos.title: Budapest Didn't Exist Until 1873 🇭🇺🤯
videos.description:
Before 1873, you could stare at Pest from Buda... and still be stuck for days.
Buda and Pest sat on opposite banks of the Danube with no permanent bridge. After a young count missed his father's funeral because of the ice, the Chain Bridge was built in 1849, and in 1873 the cities merged with a third town, Óbuda, to become Budapest.

videos.title: Russia And America Are Secretly Neighbours?!
videos.description:
Russia and the USA are just 3.8 km apart, and almost a whole day apart in time.

In the Bering Strait, Russia's Big Diomede and America's Little Diomede sit 3.8 km apart. The border was set between them in 1867, when the US bought Alaska from Russia for $7.2 million. That border is also the International Date Line, so Big Diomede runs 20 to 21 hours ahead, which is why they're nicknamed Tomorrow Island and Yesterday Island.

Map data: Natural Earth.

videos.title: Egypt is mysterious!
videos.description:
95% of Egyptians live within 20 km of one river. Here's why.

Cairo gets about 2.5 cm of rain a year, yet the Nile never runs dry. For thousands of years, monsoon rain on Ethiopia's mountains rushed down the Blue Nile and flooded Egypt every summer, leaving the black mud that gave the country its ancient name: Kemet, the Black Land. The Aswan High Dam tamed the flood in 1970, but Egypt still lives on that thin green line.

videos.title: Are There UFOs In America?
videos.description:
In the late 1950s, UFO sightings over America shot up. Decades later, the CIA said: "It was us."

In 1955 the CIA picked Groom Lake, a dry salt flat in the Nevada desert (today's Area 51), to test its new U-2 spy plane. The U-2 flew above 60,000 feet (about 18 km), while airliners of the time flew at 10,000–20,000 feet. At sunset its silver wings still caught the sunlight, so pilots far below reported fiery objects. CIA officials later estimated that over half of all UFO reports from the late 1950s and 1960s were these spy flights.

videos.title: Earth’s Loneliest Spot is !
videos.description:
There's a place on Earth where the closest humans are in space.

Point Nemo, in the South Pacific, is 2,688 km from the nearest land, so when the International Space Station passes about 400 km overhead, its crew are the nearest people. That emptiness is why space agencies have sunk around 260 spacecraft there since 1971, including six Salyut stations and Mir, and the ISS is due to follow around 2030. Plus the Bloop, and the sunken city Lovecraft placed about 300 km away.

Map data: Natural Earth.

videos.title: You've Been Saying Everest WRONG
videos.description:
The highest mountain on Earth is named after a man who never saw it, and he didn't even want the name.

In the mid-1800s, the Survey of India measured a Himalayan summit from about 160 km away and called it Peak XV. After Radhanath Sikdar's calculations showed it was the highest, Andrew Waugh named it after his old boss, George Everest, who objected. And Everest said his own name "EEV-rist".

videos.title: Dinosaurs Could Still Be Living Today #geography #dinosaur
videos.description:
The asteroid that killed the dinosaurs had just a 13% chance of doing it.

66 million years ago, a 10 km asteroid struck what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, on rock packed with oil and sulphur that became Sun-blocking soot and gas. One study found that only 13% of Earth's surface could have caused the mass extinction. At the same time, the Deccan Traps were erupting in western India, and the black rock under Mumbai and Pune comes from them.

videos.title: Your Water May Be Older Than the Sun 🤯
videos.description:
Up to half the water you drink may be older than the Sun.

Pull every drop off Earth – oceans, ice, groundwater, even the water in you – and it forms a ball just 1,385 km wide. Every lake and river on the planet fits in a ball only 56 km across. Yet Jupiter's moon Europa may hold twice the water of Earth's oceans, and a quasar 12 billion light-years away is wrapped in 140 trillion times more.
